title: Variant + treats a numeric string as a number; & treats it as a string. Same expression returns 8 or '53' depending on the operator
sourceContent:
Attribute VB_Name = "modPricing"
Option Explicit

' Demonstrates the classic VB6 Variant-operator trap.
' AddV("5", 3) returns the Variant 8  (numeric add — + coerces String→Long).
' CatV("5", 3) returns the String  "53" (string concat — & coerces Long→String).
' The C# port that uses + with mixed types will silently produce different output.

Public Function AddV(ByVal a As Variant, ByVal b As Variant) As Variant
    AddV = a + b
End Function

Public Function CatV(ByVal a As Variant, ByVal b As Variant) As Variant
    CatV = a & b
End Function

canonicalInputs.rationale: + on String 5 + Long 3 coerces String→Long via Variant arithmetic.
& on String 5 + Long 3 coerces Long→String via concatenation.
+ commutative under the same coercion rule.
+ fails to coerce 'abc' to Long; behaviour is documented but rarely tested.

notes: Top-of-list silent-drift trap for any LLM-only port. The C# `+` operator on `object + int` will not produce 8 for the String '5' — it will throw or concatenate via `ToString`, depending on operand order. The extraction MUST emit (a) both INV claims naming the operator behaviour, (b) edge_case claims pinning the canonical examples '5'+3=8 and '5'&3='53', and (c) a default_property_usage claim explaining the implicit Variant.Value coercion on the & path. Missing the operator-vs-operand distinction is a calibration miss.
